titre: The Coleman Report (1966): Schools Don't Matter, Really?
accroche: In 1966, a report on 645,000 students finds that differences between schools explain little of the differences between students. It was read as: schools don't matter.
contenu_vulgarise:
In July 1966, a report submitted under the direction of the sociologist James Coleman was supposed, according to the sociologists Adam Gamoran and Daniel Long, to document what most took for granted: if poor children and Black children do less well, it is because their schools lack resources. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 had called for a national survey on the inequality of educational opportunity. The report, *Equality of Educational Opportunity*, finds something else, and what is mostly remembered is a sentence that Gamoran and Long relate: S. M. Lipset supposedly told Daniel Moynihan that, according to Coleman, schools make no difference and families are what make the difference.

## The Mechanism

The data were collected in September and October 1965 in 4,000 American public schools. All students in the third, sixth, ninth, and twelfth grades of the American system (the “grades,” which do not correspond to French school years) took part, along with first graders in half of the schools: more than 645,000 students in all. About 30% of the selected schools did not participate. The report sets the results of standardized tests against the characteristics of the schools: libraries, laboratories, curricula, teacher qualities, the background of the other students.

Its first finding, in the summary: once the socioeconomic background of the students is taken into account, schools are remarkably alike in their relationship to outcomes, and the differences between schools explain only a small fraction of the differences in outcomes between students. The variation between students within the same school is about four times greater than that between schools. Gamoran and Long detail a calculation from the report: in ninth grade, the five groups of school factors explain 8% of the variation in verbal outcomes, against 38% when two family variables and one student attitude variable are added.

## What It Shifts

The report does not say that school has no effect. Gamoran and Long write that this did not mean that schools make no difference: according to later research, they matter a great deal for learning. The summary itself notes that the achievement of minority students (other than Asian Americans) depends more on the school attended than that of white students: 20% of the achievement of Black students in the South is associated with the specific school they attend, against 10% for white students in the South. It concludes that it is for the most disadvantaged children that improving school would make the most difference. Among the five groups of school factors, it is the school's student body, that is, the background of the other students, that explains the largest share.

What the report establishes, according to Gamoran and Long, is that the gaps in resources between schools weighed little on the gaps between students. Mosteller and Moynihan note that these resources varied little from one school to another, notably between the schools attended by Black students and by white students; this slight variation limits what they can explain. Gamoran and Long also recall the methodological criticisms: a study at a single point in time, relationships assumed to be linear and additive, percentages of variation explained that depend on the assumed causal order among the variables.

The report therefore says little about what resources would do if they varied much more from one school to another.

repere.texte: Of 4,000 schools and more than 645,000 students surveyed in fall 1965, the variation in outcomes between students within the same school is about four times that between schools; 20% of the achievement of Black students in the South is associated with their school, against 10% for white students in the South.
repere.source: Coleman et al., Equality of Educational Opportunity, U.S. Office of Education, 1966, summary, pp. 21-23

carte.punch: The Coleman report is summed up as: schools don't matter. It says something narrower.
carte.idee: The 1966 report (more than 645,000 students) finds that differences between schools explain little of the differences in outcomes between students, in schools with little difference in resources. It does not say that school has no effect: improving it would make more difference for disadvantaged students.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The summary takes up the first pages; the complete report runs to more than seven hundred pages.

quiz.question: Why does the Coleman report, which compares schools, find that their differences explain little of student outcomes?
choix: Because the schools surveyed all had exactly the same resources and the same student body
Because the tests used did not cover the subjects actually taught in these schools
Because the investigators measured only the students and collected no data on the schools
Because students within the same school differ far more from one another than schools do from each other
quiz.explication: The variation between students within the same school is about four times that between schools, and resources varied little from one school to another. The schools were not identical, the report did collect data on them, and nothing in the summary calls the tests into question. This does not mean that school has no effect.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What called for the survey that produced the Coleman report?
choix: A 1954 Supreme Court decision on school desegregation
The Civil Rights Act of 1964, which called for a survey on the inequality of educational opportunity
A personal initiative of James Coleman, with no legal mandate
An earlier Senate report on the funding of public schools
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 had called for a national survey on the inequality of educational opportunity: it is what produced the 1966 report.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the report, for which students is the school attended most associated with achievement?
choix: Black students in the South, for whom school weighs twice as much as for white students in the South
White students in the South, whose achievement depends almost entirely on school
Minority students of Asian origin, whose results vary the most from school to school
All students in the same way, whatever their origin
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The report associates school with 20% of the achievement of Black students in the South, against only 10% for white students in the South, that is, twice as much.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Among the report's five groups of school factors, which explains the largest share of outcomes?
choix: Facilities, such as libraries and laboratories
Teacher quality, measured independently of the students
The school's student body, that is, the background of the other students
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The report identifies the school's student body, that is, the background of the other students, as the school factor that weighs most on outcomes.
